manufacturers.short_history: 360 Systems is a Californian electronics manufacturer founded in 1972 by Robert "Bob" Bruce Easton, a USC cinema graduate working in the Hollywood film industry, on a business plan of applying new semiconductor technology to products for the music and recording industries. It belongs in this database for its late 1970s and 1980s musical instruments: the Spectre Guitar Synthesizer of 1979, the 360 Systems Digital Keyboard of the early 1980s, which played sampled sounds stored one per EPROM chip and is described as the first synthesizer to carry sampled sounds on integrated circuits, and the MIDI Bass and MIDI Bass Pro sound modules that put library bass samples under MIDI control. The company left the musical instrument market and moved into professional audio playback and then broadcast video servers, which it still builds today from its headquarters in Newbury Park, California; none of that broadcast product line is in scope here.
manufacturers.long_history:
360 Systems was founded in 1972 by Robert "Bob" Bruce Easton (1945 to 2021), a graduate of the University of Southern California cinema department who was working in the Hollywood film industry. The company's own history page states that the original business plan focused on applying new semiconductor technology to products for the music and recording industries, and that several of the firsts that came out of the 1970s work later became industry standards. The company is a privately held California corporation and designs and manufactures at its headquarters in Newbury Park, California.

The early catalogue mixed instruments with studio tools. 360 Systems lists a Frequency Shifter in 1976, the Spectre Guitar Synthesizer in 1979 and a Programmable Parametric Equalizer in 1980, the last of these aimed at recording studios and live sound rather than at players. Of these only the Spectre is a sound generating instrument. The company then names the 360 Keyboard, the MIDI Bass and the MIDI Patcher as its later popular music products of the early to mid 1980s.

The 360 Systems Digital Keyboard, produced in small numbers between 1982 and 1984, was a 49 key, eight voice instrument whose sounds were held in ROM, each sound on its own integrated circuit plugged into a ZIF socket on one of three internal boards. Its library covered Mellotron strings and flutes alongside Bosendorfer grand piano, vibraphone, guitars, fretless and slap bass, brass and woodwinds, and an expensive sixteen piece string orchestra chip. It could be split across the keyboard or layered in unison, and it is described as the first synthesizer to feature sampled sounds on IC chips, comparable in role to a Mellotron, Chamberlin or Orchestron but with higher fidelity and more control.

The MIDI Bass followed in 1986 as a dedicated monophonic bass expander in a small metal box, marketed with the slogan "Real Bass In A Box" because it played recorded rather than synthesized bass. Sounds again lived on EPROMs, up to four at a time, with a MIDI channel selector and a key priority switch offering last, low and high key modes so the bass line could track a particular part of a performance. It was sold in two and four sound models, its audio bandwidth ran from 16 Hz to 16 kHz, and a June 1986 magazine review lists a starting library including picked and snapped Fender Jazz bass, stand up finger picked bass and a MiniMoog or Oberheim style synth bass, with 27 further sound chips available separately. The rack mounted MIDI Bass Pro of 1987 answered what players had asked for, with a megabyte of internal EPROM sound memory, a signal to noise ratio in excess of 90 dB and two 12 MHz processors handling internal operations.

After the instrument years the company turned to professional audio playback and then broadcast. Its Permanent Playback digital audio message players of the 1980s stored audio on EPROM chips and became a fixture in theme parks, the DigiCart hard disk audio recorder and player opened the broadcast equipment business, the Instant Replay audio clip player first shipped in 1994, and from 2003 the Image Server, MAXX and TSS families made the company a video server manufacturer. That broadcast and pro AV line, including the current DigiCart 5 and Instant Replay 3, is outside the scope of this database.

manufacturers.review_note: Deliberately left out as not sound generating: the Frequency Shifter (1976, effect unit), the Programmable Parametric Equalizer (1980, studio EQ), the MIDI Patcher (MIDI routing), the Permanent Playback message players, and the whole broadcast and pro AV line (DigiCart, Instant Replay, Short/cut, Ethernet Audio, Image Server, MAXX, TSS time delay servers). A web search summary also mentioned an earlier 360 Systems Slavedriver pitch to CV and gate converter, said to be around 1977 and connected to a collaboration with Tom Oberheim; that claim is left out entirely because the page it came from (electronicmusic.fandom.com) returned HTTP 402 and could not be fetched, and a pitch to CV converter generates no sound in any case. It is also unresolved which product actually came first: the company's own 50 years page captions the 1976 Frequency Shifter as the "First 360 Systems product", which is not the same as the Slavedriver claim; a human should check this against a fetchable source. long_name is null because no source gives a legal entity name beyond "360 Systems" and "a privately held California corporation". Wikidata search for "360 Systems" returns zero entities, so there is no wikidata tier source. The Digital Keyboard is called "360 Keyboard" and "Midi Keyboard, early 1980's" on the company page and "Digital Keyboard" on synth-db; the 1982 year and the 1982 to 1984 production run come from synth-db only, so a second source would be useful. synth-db and vintagesynth are secondary sources, tier "other". The synth-db URLs contain literal spaces exactly as the site serves them.

manufacturers.short_history: Manikin Electronic is a small Berlin manufacturer of electronic music hardware, trading under the partnership Thorsten Feuerherdt & Markus Horn GbR at Lipaer Strasse 5 in 12203 Berlin, and using the motto "Elektronische Musikmaschinen aus Berlin" since 2003, the year it launched its first product. It is in this database for the Memotron, which the company calls the world's first digital Mellotron: a keyboard that plays a large library of samples taken from original 1960s and 1970s Mellotron tapes, laid out to match the classic Mellotron 400 front panel. The Memotron appeared as a keyboard and later as a rack unit, and was reworked in 2016 into the more powerful m2k keyboard and m2d desktop, which remain the current models. The company's first product, the Schrittmacher step sequencer, and its later Eurorack and pro audio interface modules are not sound generating and are therefore not listed as instruments.
manufacturers.long_history:
Manikin Electronic is run as a German civil law partnership, Thorsten Feuerherdt & Markus Horn GbR, based at Lipaer Strasse 5, 12203 Berlin. Its own site dates the company motto, "Elektronische Musikmaschinen aus Berlin", to 2003, the year it brought its first product to market: the Schrittmacher, a step sequencer designed to be operated intuitively and to suit live use. More than twenty years later the company says the Schrittmacher is still popular. It offers 32 parameter lines of 16 steps each, freely configurable and linkable, driven from 16 endless encoders with push function and 28 buttons.

The product that made the company known outside sequencer circles is the Memotron, which Manikin describes as the world's first digital Mellotron. It is a digital remake of the Mellotron: the case, the classic white styling and the layout of the controls follow the Mellotron 400, with knobs for volume, tone, pitch and sound selection, a half speed switch, a data controller and an escape button, a small LCD, 37 lightweight unweighted keys, headphone and stereo outputs, volume pedal input and MIDI In, Out and Thru. Where the original was a tape replay instrument, the Memotron plays samples, offers up to three sounds at once, includes an adjustable internal effect processor with reverb, delay, chorus and flanging algorithms, and can take further sounds from external storage. A Sound On Sound review of the original model reports that the sound library derives from Klaus Hoffmann's large collection of Mellotron tapes, recorded at a 32 kHz sample rate with minimal processing, no normalisation and only sparing de-noising, so that wow and flutter, level differences and unstable pitch survive as part of the character. The company deliberately keeps those artefacts in its Sound Collections for the same reason.

The Memotron line grew over time. The company's own archive page dates the Memotron Keyboard to 2007 through 2015 and the Memotron Rack to 2010 through 2016. In 2016 the range went into a second, more powerful round with the m2k keyboard and the m2d desktop, the latter housing the classic M400 control panel in a robust metal desktop case. Sound Collections beyond the included Basic Collection cover both famous Mellotron sounds and unusual custom material, and since 2024 they are sold as digital downloads. Manikin lists Deep Purple, King Crimson and Tangerine Dream among the users of the Memotron.

Since 2018 the catalogue has also included Eurorack modules, and more recently a Pro Audio Bricks range co-developed with Lake People. None of these generate sound: modul 1 is an eight channel USB AD and DA converter with MIDI, modul 2 a USB high speed isolator, modul 3 a transformer isolator and DI box, modul 4 a dual headphone amplifier, modul 5 a phono preamplifier, while the Pro Audio Bricks are a 10 MHz reference clock generator and a USB isolator.

conflicts.description: The manufacturer's own site says the Memotron was introduced in 2007, and its archive page dates the Memotron Keyboard to 2007 through 2015; vintagesynth also says Manikin stepped up in 2007. English Wikipedia instead says the instrument debuted at the NAMM Show in 2006. Because the two claims give different years the year is left null here. The likely reconciliation is a 2006 trade show debut followed by a 2007 market release, but no source read here states that, so a human should confirm before filling the year.

manufacturers.review_note: founders is null on purpose. The Impressum names Thorsten Feuerherdt and Markus Horn as the partners of the GbR that trades as Manikin Electronic, but no source read here calls them the founders, so the field is left empty rather than inferred; a human can promote it if that inference is acceptable. founded_year 2003 rests on the company's own wording, "This has been our motto since 2003, the year we launched our first product", which is a first product date rather than an explicit incorporation date. Deliberately left out of the instruments array: the Schrittmacher step sequencer (2003), because a sequencer generates no sound, even though it is the company's first and still current product and its historical importance is covered in the history text; the Eurorack modules modul 1 to modul 5 (USB AD/DA and MIDI interface, USB isolator, transformer isolator, dual headphone amplifier, phono preamplifier), all non sound generating; the Pro Audio Bricks 10MHz4Reference master clock and Isolator4USB, co-developed with Lake People; the Memotron Sound Collections, which are sound content rather than instruments; and the CV-DAC USB to CV interface mentioned by a dealer listing. No software instrument was found on the official site, so no software product had to be suppressed under the hardware only rule, but the site was only read at Home, Products index, Eurorack, Pro Audio Bricks, Archive and Impressum level, so a human may want to check the shop. Wikidata search for "Manikin Electronic" returns zero entities and German Wikipedia has no article on the company, only a Mellotron article that mentions the Memotron in passing, so there is no wikidata tier source and no native language encyclopedia entry. The relations array is empty because the Lake People co-development is neither supplier, owner_of, acquired_by nor subsidiary_of; if a partnership relation type is added later, that link belongs there. vintagesynth and Sound On Sound are secondary sources, tier "other".
